articles.title_orig: Supreme Court blocks Missouri congressional map favoring GOP for third time
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court blocks Missouri congressional map favoring GOP for third time
articles.content_orig:
Court puts end to long-running legal dispute as it rules Republican-friendly map cannot be used in November
The supreme court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by Donald Trump , putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is under way in the midterm elections.
The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.
The supreme court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri supreme court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.
“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. “The district court and court of appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri.”
Republicans had hoped the new House map – which already was used in the August primaries – could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.
A panel of the eighth US circuit court of appeals ruled on Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the US constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order’s effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the supreme court.
The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters – nearly one in four statewide – who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts, though some local election officials had urged voters to wait because of the legal uncertainty.
Republicans currently hold six of Missouri’s eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican governor Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.
The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by longtime Democratic congressman Emanuel Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s fifth congressional district far eastward into rural Republican areas.
The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri’s other congressional districts.
Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state senator Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican congressman Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the eighth circuit’s ruling and the last two appeals to the supreme court.
At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri’s congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their US House districts over the past year.
Missouri’s new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact . In one case, the Missouri supreme court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.
Republican secretary of state Denny Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on 4 August – the day the new districts were used in the primaries – to reject the petition. He asserted referendum petitions aren’t allowed for congressional redistricting.
The Missouri supreme court ruled on 3 September that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The supreme court let that ruling stand on 8 September. But minutes later, US district judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.
The supreme court on 10 September blocked Clark’s order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri supreme court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark’s order.
But that wasn’t the end of the matter. The eighth circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark’s blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That’s what led to the latest decision from the US supreme court.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms
articles.content_orig:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.
Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.
"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.
Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.
He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".
"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.
A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".
Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached
The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief.
It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.
But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.
However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.
The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.
The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations. US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has requested military support from Trump.
On Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and drones launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia.
During his speech at the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
On Friday, Araghchi said Iran did not accept "coercion, threats or intimidation" and added that "peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation".

The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee , the network says.
Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network , along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.
In the latest roadblock, the White House announced in a Friday night note detailing the president’s schedule that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported .
CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks. No other outlet was listed to replace CNN in the memo, according to the network. Without a designated pooler, major networks won’t be able to televise his trip.
The network’s journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported .
The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.
MS NOW also reported being blocked from the greeting ceremony. “The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López asked network host Symone Sanders Townsend Thursday night.
But CNN was allowed to cover Trump and Xi’s visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.
The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network’s coverage of Trump’s Knoxville trip.
Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them “fake news.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social.
The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.
In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.
But reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.
The White House TV press pool had abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned until their access was reinstated. CBS served as the designated pooler Friday, filming Xi and Trump at the White House during the final day of his state visit .
Trump’s disdain for the mainstream press is well-documented, including his outbursts at female journalists for asking questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war. He has repeatedly targeted CNN’s Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins for “not smiling.”
But his attempt to ban several major outlets from the White House is unprecedented.
Former President Bill Clinton — who had an affair with a young staffer, Monica Lewinsky , in the 1990s that dominated the news cycle — said at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.
“And there's a reason we have a Constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

President Trump has reportedly rejected a seven-day cease-fire proposed by Iran and expects to resume bombing the country after the midterm elections.
As part of the proposed cease-fire, Tehran pledged to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations on dismantling its nuclear program in exchange for the US ending its blockade of Iranian ports.
However, Trump is “skeptical” Iran will agree to his demands and has told aides it is “likely” the US military restarts airstrikes after the November contests, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing US officials.
It’s unclear what level of strikes Trump is planning on launching.
Trump also trolled Iran on Friday night, sharing a map of the Persian Gulf region on Truth Social with the Strait of Hormuz circled and labeled “Trump Strait.”
In his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week, Trump warned that with peace negotiations stalled, he could choose to “annihilate” Iran.
The president has previously threatened to destroy “civilization” in Iran and bomb the country’s bridges and energy infrastructure, but has largely stopped short of launching those types of attacks.
Iran floated the possibility of a seven-day cease-fire during a meeting with mediators in Qatar on Sunday, the outlet reported.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the UN gathering in New York that the seven-day proposal had been formally offered to the US.
Aside from lifting the naval blockade, the regime is also seeking sanctions relief from the US and the unfreezing of some of its assets.
A White House official told Reuters earlier this week that the “crushing sanctions” and “one of the most successful blockades in history” have crippled Iran’s economy and left the country broke.
The official noted that Trump was content to allow the “inevitable Iranian collapse” play out rather than be “played” by the regime.
US officials have conveyed to Iran that Trump has “no intention” of lifting the naval blockade, according to the Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: Trump cancels $1B in federal spending in latest challenge to Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump cancels $1B in federal spending in latest challenge to Congress
articles.content_orig:
President using rare power to revoke expenditure with bipartisan approval to aid immigrant services
Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s office of management and budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending”.
Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic president Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by senator Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Collins said in a statement the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions”.
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
“This is theft from the American people, plain and simple,” Patty Murray, the Washington Democratic senator, who is vice-chair of the appropriations committee said in a statement . “These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people – not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families. Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because [Russell] Vought is saying their votes don’t count.”
Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The government accountability office has called the maneuver , known as a “pocket rescission,” illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse”.
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9bn in congressionally approved foreign aid. The US supreme court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a pocket rescission fits part of a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the US government, eroding the power of Congress.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court lets Trump administration use revamped federal voter eligibility database for now
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court lets Trump administration use revamped federal voter eligibility database for now
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.
Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.
But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.
On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.
The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.
In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.
In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.
Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.
The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.
Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.
The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.
The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.
The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.
After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune .
Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.
In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.
Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.

articles.title_orig: The Major Social Media Platforms Are All Rejecting Paid Ads for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ (Exclusive)
articles.title_zh: The Major Social Media Platforms Are All Rejecting Paid Ads for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ (Exclusive)
articles.content_orig:
Senior Editor, Technology and Politics
So much for free speech. The studio releasing Alex Gibney ’s new Elon Musk documentary Musk is finding itself unable to buy an ad on the biggest social platforms. YouTube , TikTok , and Instagram and Facebook owner Meta are all declining to run the trailer for Musk , along with X itself, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. That last one is perhaps understandable, given its owner. But the rejection by the other platforms has taken distributor Bleecker Street by surprise, and it is internally scrambling to understand why the ad has been rejected, according to a person familiar with the company’s processes who is not authorized to talk about them publicly. The unwillingness of platforms to accept even paid advertising is sure to raise concerns about free speech and the dwindling number of companies that control many of the platforms in this country — and ironically provide a proof-text for the very point the film is coming to make. Gibney’s doc is a four-hour look at a title character who attempts to control the conversation in various ways , including with alleged suppressions on X, which he bought in 2022.
Bleecker Street opens Musk in theaters on Oct. 9. YouTube, TikTok and Meta have all supplied a reason related to “political content” to Bleecker Street reps. The latter two companies’ platforms, by policy, do not allow campaign or other political ads, in Meta’s case largely owing to fallout from the Cambridge Analytica Facebook scandal during the 2016 election. But the Musk trailer, which dropped Thursday, does not appear to fall in the category of the campaign advertising those bylaws were enacted to prevent. It simply contains a shot of a political rally in 2024 and a reference at the end to the 2024 election — the kind of flicks that occur in numerous documentaries and are hardly meant to stump for a particular candidate in an upcoming race.
The reason for YouTube’s rejection is even less clear, as the platform does allow campaign ads, albeit with “paid for” disclosures from vetted candidates.
Bleecker Street has entered an appeal with all three companies. Meta has already rejected the appeal. TikTok and YouTube are still entertaining the petitions. For its part, X has refused to engage with Bleecker Street on the film or even accept advertising for any of its other films on its upcoming calendar. Press reps at Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X did not immediately provide a comment. A Bleecker Street representative confirmed that the ads were initially rejected but said they are continuing to appeal with all three companies besides X in the hope minds can be changed.
Traction on social media is key for a documentary release, which relies on word-of-mouth in a way a big-budget feature doesn’t.
The news also hits a nerve after Universal, which is releasing the film overseas, considered backing away from distributing Musk before capitulating to public pressure and commenting that it is standing by the film (though no details have yet been given).
It is unclear if there has been any communication between ad reps at X and the other social giants. Some other tech firms will also see their leaders under the Hollywood spotlight this fall, with Sony releasing Aaron Sorkin’s Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning next month. That film’s trailer is currently available on YouTube.

U.S. equities rose on Friday as Wall Street wrapped up a volatile week of trading, with a surge in Treasury yields rippling through financial markets.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.51% to close at 7,743.41, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.5% to 27,068.72. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 478.64 points, or 0.93% to end at 51,828.62.
Akamai Technologies was a key winner of the session, rising 3% after announcing a multiyear deal with Anthropic .
Also helping sentiment, oil prices slid amid optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened, as Iran has asked the U.S. to return to the memorandum of understanding from June that failed to end the Middle East conflict. West Texas Intermediate crude futures dropped 2.33% to settle at $92.41 per barrel, while international benchmark Brent crude futures declined 2.14% to $104.32 a barrel.
With the day's gains, the Dow notched a winning week, up 0.3%. The S&P 500 added 1.2%, while the Nasdaq rose 2%.
That advance was bolstered by technology stocks such as Meta Platforms , which popped nearly 13% on the week amid excitement surrounding its artificial intelligence agent Muse . Information technology rose 3.1%, which was the most of any of the S&P 500's sectors.
The drama continued in the bond market, where the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2007 , while the 30-year yield reached its highest level since 2004. The two were last seen up slightly at 5.163% and 5.488%, respectively.
This week's ascent in yields was fueled by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, persistently high energy prices due to the Iran war, and a hot purchasing managers' report. Fed funds futures trading suggests a roughly 64% likelihood of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
Eric Diton, president of The Wealth Alliance, noted that investor sentiment has been weakening as bond yields have been rising, with bearish sentiment seeing a "sharp" increase from just two weeks earlier. That said, he believes the market has been "incredibly resilient" in the face of the developments, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq roughly 1% below their recent highs.
"Should rates continue to climb, they should have a larger impact on market performance at some point in the future," he cautioned.
Meanwhile, traders were monitoring Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the U.S. this week. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC Friday that " a lot more details " on negotiations between the U.S. and China are going to be released Monday.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier in the week that the two countries have agreed to extend their trade truce by two months.
The three leading U.S. indexes finished with gains on Friday.
The S&P 500 gained 0.51% to end the session at 7,743.41, while the Nasdaq Composite moved up 0.48% to 27,068.72. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 478.64 points, or 0.93%, to 51,828.62.
Wall Street can't agree on what's driving the surge in bond yields — whether it's stubborn inflation or rapid growth or the exploding deficit — but, whatever the cause, the likelihood that higher interest rates are here to stay is unnerving investors who fear that eventually something has to break .

Stump said that despite a steeper than expected 7-7.5% decline in same-store sales this quarter, contacts were encouraged by changes being made by Wendy's new C-Suite, including CEO Bob Wright's willingness to admit to the challenges the chain faced lately and CFO Steve Cirulis' previous success in turning around sandwich chain Potbelly along with Wright.

"Corporate is planning to roll out a new everyday value construct in October that will replace WEN's existing Biggie Bags platform. While details are not yet known, our contacts are confident the upcoming everyday value transformation will be far more compelling to consumers," the note read.
The fast food franchise has faced a tumultuous year. Riyadh is exporting 6 million barrels per day in September, the highest level since the Iran war began about seven months ago. The kingdom's crude shipments have recovered to the monthly average of 2025.

articles.title_zh: Ex-American Idol contestant told lover he dreamed of killing wife, murder trial hears
articles.content_orig:
Alleigha Botner tells court Caleb Flynn, charged with murder of wife Ashley Flynn, sent her AI love songs
The Ohio former pastor and American Idol contestant accused of fatally shooting his wife fantasized to his then lover about killing his spouse and sent her AI-generated love songs, according to evidence presented at trial this week.
Caleb Flynn, 40, is on trial for aggravated murder in connection with the 16 February shooting death of Ashley Flynn. He also is charged with two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence, according to a March indictment. Flynn has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Prosecutors say Flynn – motivated by a desire to be with his girlfriend, Alleigha Botner – shot his sleeping wife twice in the back of the head. He allegedly altered the crime scene to look like a deadly home invasion.
Flynn’s defense team has acknowledged the affair, but said at trial it does not make him a murderer. “A man can make selfish decisions without committing a crime,” defense attorney Emily Smith said.
Investigators recovered songs from Flynn’s phone, where he reflected on his friendship with Botner evolving into a romantic relationship.
“That first time I saw you the room disappeared, love at first sight even though I was scared,” a voice sang in a style reminiscent of Christian rock, according to video broadcast by Court TV. “Life is now empty, since the moment I lost you,” the song ended.
A second version with similar lyrics but delivered in a somber tone was also played to the court.
Botner was 20 when she met Flynn at their church, Botner testified. Flynn was 36 or 37 at the time.
“At first it was: I want her dead. I wish she was gone. And then it was: if I could kill her and not go to jail, I would. And one night, he was up really late – he told me he was thinking about ways to kill her,” Botner, now 24, said.
Flynn also repeatedly said he hated his wife in several texts to Botner.
During an August 2025 cruise to celebrate the married couple’s 15th wedding anniversary, Ashley Flynn found texts her husband had sent to Botner. She tried to arrange a coffee meet-up with Botner. Botner avoided the conversation, saying she was busy.
In January, Botner gave Caleb Flynn an ultimatum: leave your wife or it’s over.
At about this time, Flynn sent her the AI-generated songs.
On 14 February, two days before Ashley was shot, Botner testified that Flynn said he was getting a divorce and would finally be free of his wife, to which Botner said she did not believe him. “I told him that I don’t trust him and that I’m moving on with my life,” she said on the stand.
When Ashley Flynn was found dead, her sister Kayla Keyt did not have knowledge of the affair. She told police when Caleb was arrested that they had the wrong guy. “I trusted Caleb with everything I had in me … He was completely innocent. I really believed that with all of my heart,” Keyt said.
The FBI subsequently informed her of the affair.
Keyt said news of the affair made the couple’s two daughters “mostly broken-hearted for mommy”.
“They said she loved daddy more than anyone else in life. So why did daddy not love her as much?” she testified.
Flynn appeared briefly on American Idol’s 12th season in 2013, describing music as his passion and saying his wife nudged him to go on the show.
The trial, which is expected to wrap by the end of next week, will resume on Monday.

articles.content_orig:
If you download the latest Google Messages update you might not notice anything different at a first glance. However, the brand has introduced several new redesigns that should make the experience more seamless with day-to-day use.
9to5Google shared the changes, giving users a heads-up that it's now even easier to gain access to timestamps in Messages. While you used to have to tap each chat bubble, you can now swipe left across the chat screen to reveal timestamps for all the messages.
It will also show the status, whether it's been delivered or pending, and whether it's secure or not. In order to reply to a message, you will now have to swipe right into the chat bubble. This might take some getting used to, but once you get it down, it should make the overall process much smoother.
In addition, Android Authority shared news about a new long-press command that's now available to experiment with in Messages. While you used to have to tap the menu at the top of a chat to access expanded features, that all changes today.
Going forward, users can long-press a message to open the same menu. The menu will provide quick access to Replay, Forward, Copy, Star, Delete, Select more, and Info. You can also long-press to highlight parts of a message if you want to copy and paste specific text.
Users can now update the app to see whether they have access. Although it's rolling out more widely, it doesn't appear to be available to everyone. For the most part, these two changes are very welcome, providing quality-of-life improvements that we can all enjoy.
Google Messages is still one of the best messaging options. However, that doesn't mean that it can't be improved. We love when Google pushes out changes, and more so when the changes are impactful. Of course, we've discovered that some tweaks need to be done on our own.
If you're looking to refine the Google Messages experience, we highly recommend checking out our in-depth guide , which will quickly and effectively clean it up. You can always try an alternative if you're looking, but those seem to be hit or miss.

articles.title_orig: Wisconsin frat leaders arrested after 30 pledges found in filthy basement, injured and covered in condiments
articles.title_zh: Wisconsin frat leaders arrested after 30 pledges found in filthy basement, injured and covered in condiments
articles.content_orig:
Two leaders of an underground University of Wisconsin-Madison fraternity were arrested and charged with hazing after dozens of pledges were found injured, shirtless and covered in condiments in a sweltering basement.
The Madison Police Department said Thursday it received an anonymous tip about an event in the basement of an off-campus chapter house.
Alpha Epsilon Pi was kicked off campus as a recognized chapter in 2015, but the organization maintained a presence at the Madison home.
Police say about 30 pledges, most of whom were 18, were found partially-clothed in a filthy basement around 8:20 p.m. on Wednesday.
The apparent hazing victims were “covered in food, condiments, and other liquids” and “had visible injuries consistent with being physically assaulted.” The thermostat was set to 81 degrees, making the basement hot and humid, police said.
Brayden Klein and Samuel Vane, both 20, were charged with hazing and disorderly conduct. Madison police are still investigating the matter.
Klein and Vane each posted $400 bail around 1 a.m. on Thursday morning and were released from the Dane County Jail, officials confirmed. It was not immediately clear when they must appear in court to face the charges.
Klein and Vane could not immediately be reached by NBC News for comment.
The university said in a statement that while it stopped recognizing Alpha Epsilon Pi about a decade ago, the national organization has continued to recognize the Madison chapter, allowing it to exist in the community.
The University of Wisconsin-Madison said in a statement that it will investigate students “implicated in the incident.”
Alpha Epsilon Pi was founded as a Jewish fraternity in 1913.
The national organization’s website lists a Madison, Wisconsin, chapter called “Pi,” but it does not cite an affiliation with the university.
In a statement, the national fraternity said it is taking the allegations “extremely seriously” and said it would “cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter.”
“Any member found responsible for criminal conduct in this matter will be expelled from AEPi, and we will support prosecution to the fullest extent of the law,” the statement said. “We will also work with the university in hopes that they will take action against individual perpetrators for violation of the student code of conduct.”
“Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for ... Anyone who engages in hazing forfeits the privilege of being an AEPi brother,” the statement continued.
Anti-hazing advocates say underground chapters present a unique risk for hazing incidents because they are not monitored by officials at their college or university.
There have been almost 130 hazing-related deaths with an average of five per year in the U.S. since 2000, according to HazingInfo.org, a research and advocacy website that tracks incidents.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.

NEW YORK (WABC) -- A powerful and long-lasting nor'easter is beginning to take shape across the Tri-State area, bringing the threat of damaging winds, significant coastal flooding, heavy rain, travel disruptions and potential power outages through the weekend.
Conditions will steadily deteriorate as the storm strengthens, with its peak impact expected from Saturday into early Sunday before slowly weakening. Even then, hazardous conditions are expected to linger into Monday.
The biggest concerns with this storm are strong winds and coastal flooding. Widespread wind gusts of 30 to 50 mph are expected across the region, while coastal communities could see gusts exceeding 60 mph. Those winds may be strong enough to bring down tree limbs, topple vulnerable trees and cause scattered power outages. Travel conditions are also expected to worsen, with delays and cancellations already beginning at area airports as the storm approaches.
Along the shoreline, expect widespread moderate coastal flooding with several locations likely to experience major flooding during high tide cycles. Breaking waves could exceed 12 feet, causing beach erosion and damaging coastal infrastructure. Areas along the South Shore of Long Island, portions of Staten Island, Queens and other vulnerable waterfront communities face some of the greatest flood risks as repeated high tides coincide with the storm's strongest winds.
Rainfall will add to the storm's impact, although it is not the primary threat. Periods of rain will move through the area in waves, with the heaviest downpours expected Saturday night into early Sunday. Most locations are forecast to receive 2 to 4 inches of rain, with isolated spots potentially seeing higher totals. While widespread river flooding is not expected, localized street flooding and ponding on roadways are likely, especially during heavier bursts of rain.
This will not be a storm that delivers constant heavy rain every hour. Instead, conditions will fluctuate with bands of rain and occasional breaks. However, even during lulls, gusty winds and hazardous coastal conditions will remain in place, making outdoor activities difficult and potentially dangerous.
Saturday is expected to be the most impactful day, featuring windswept rain, damaging coastal winds and increasing coastal flooding. Conditions may worsen Saturday night as the storm delivers its heaviest rainfall and strongest impacts. By Sunday, the system will begin to slowly unwind, but periods of rain, gusty winds and continued coastal flooding are still expected.
The storm's influence should finally begin to fade on Monday, although lingering light rain and cloudy skies may persist through part of the day. Drier weather is expected to return Tuesday, with a more pleasant pattern developing later next week. Forecasters say temperatures could climb back above 70 degrees as September transitions into October, bringing a stretch of quieter weather after a turbulent weekend.
Officials are urging residents in flood-prone areas to monitor high tide schedules, stay informed of local emergency management recommendations and prepare for the possibility of coastal flooding, power outages and hazardous travel conditions as the nor'easter moves through the region.

articles.title_orig: Jury finds Facebook liable for deceiving users in Cambridge Analytica case
articles.title_zh: Jury finds Facebook liable for deceiving users in Cambridge Analytica case
articles.content_orig:
A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections on the social media platform.
It is now up to the judge to determine how much the company would pay, with attorneys representing the state asking for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.
The two-week trial in Santa Fe centered on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica , to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for President Trump.
Jurors sided with prosecutors, finding Facebook's failure to protect users' data impacted New Mexico's entire population of more than 2 million people.
"For years, Facebook operated as if the rules that apply to everyone else didn't apply to them. Today, a jury of New Mexicans said otherwise," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. "This is a historic verdict, not just for New Mexico, but for every state fighting to hold Big Tech accountable."
Jurors also found Facebook misled the public about investigations into data brokers following the Cambridge Analytica scandal , finding the company liable for over 2 million violations.
During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook claimed the state's evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico failed to find more than one other instance of a data breach.
A Meta spokesperson told CBS News the company disagreed with the jury's verdict and will continue to defend "against efforts to distort our records." The company also noted that free speech issues "featured very prominently" in the case.
"We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community," the spokesperson said. "This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users' information and giving them control over their data."
Meta agreed in August to pay up to $18 billion to settle the multistate lawsuit surrounding child safety issues. Buried in the 130-page settlement was an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach, making New Mexico the only state to pursue a case. Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, saying it was not tough enough on Meta.
Also this year, New Mexico won judgments totaling $942 million from Meta in a two-phase trial about the company's safety protections for minors. Furthermore, the court ordered Meta to implement new safeguards, including age-verification technology and time limits on its platforms.
"Let this be a warning to every technology company doing business in our state," Torrez said Friday. "If you lie to New Mexicans about how you use their data, we will find out, and we will hold you accountable."

articles.title_orig: Chris Hansen Reacts to ‘Primetime’ and Robert Pattinson’s Portrayal of Him: ‘So Bizarre’ and ‘Detached From Reality’

articles.content_orig:
Chris Hansen finally took a seat for “ Primetime ,” and he was not happy about the portrayal of himself.
The former “To Catch a Predator” host said on Fox News’ “Jesse Watters Primetime” in August that he left the offices of distributor A24 without seeing the film due to the legal agreement they wanted him to sign. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it,” he said of the agreement. He also said he found Robert Pattinson ’s impression “overly dramatic,” but that his family thought it was a “pretty good imitation.”
Now that Hansen has seen Lance Oppenheim’s drama, he is prepared to share his reaction. In a short clip filmed outside a theater, Hansen gave a teaser of his initial thoughts, with a promise to post his full reaction on his podcast and YouTube channel, “Have A Seat With Chris Hansen,” at 7 p.m. ET on Friday.
“It was so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” Hansen said. “Obviously, I’m not objective because the character is, you know, me, but it was so detached from reality or anything I’ve experienced then or now doing the investigations. I’m not sure what the point of it was.”
The film stars Pattinson as Hansen in 2006 as “To Catch a Predator” transitioned from “Dateline NBC” to its own primetime block. A24 labeled the film as “inspired by true events,” rather than a biopic.
Pattinson himself hoped Hansen would come around on the portrayal. “I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment,” the actor said following Hansen’s comments on his imitation.
“Primetime” opened this week in theaters, after making its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, where it garnered buzz and a seven-minute ovation.

articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran ‘s tour stops at Gillette Stadium have been canceled.
The shows, set to take place on Friday and Saturday nights at the Foxborough, Massachusetts, venue, have been axed due to a nor’easter headed up the East Coast.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” tour promoter Messina Touring Group said in a statement.
“The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The cancellation comes as Sheeran soldiers on solo with his Loop Tour after opening act Macklemore was dropped from the lineup following criticism of his “Free Palestine” remarks at two MetLife Stadium shows earlier this month. Fellow opening acts Finneas O’Connell, Danish band Lukas Graham, Irish band Beoga and singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe have also left the tour.
Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft was among those who objected to Macklemore’s comments, and he suggested that Macklemore wasn’t welcome at the Foxborough, Massachusetts, shows for what Kraft considered “hate speech.” Macklemore also claimed that Kraft rallied other stadium owners and told Sheeran that if the rapper stayed on the tour, Sheeran wouldn’t be allowed to play at their venues.
“Gillette Stadium has a longstanding commitment to providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech,” Kraft said in part in a statement released after Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s tour and the rapper had indicated the influential New England Patriots owner was involved in the decision. “Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line. This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf. Their pain and loss are real. But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas, a United States and globally … designated terrorist organization whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.”
The Wall Street Journal later reported that Kraft and other NFL stadium owners reached out to Messina Touring Group after Macklemore’s first “Free Palestine” remarks at his Sept. 4 MetLife Stadium show and were assured he wouldn’t bring up the issue again. But Macklemore repeated his comments during the second MetLife Stadium show.
Messina Touring Group dropped Macklemore from the tour on Sept. 14, saying venues would not allow the concerts to take place with the rapper on the lineup.
“As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” Messina Touring Group said in its statement announcing Macklemore being dropped from the tour. “After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.”

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Said to Have Been Warned by Emirati Leader About Hamas Attack Before Oct. 7
articles.content_orig:
Displaced Palestinians shelter near a damaged tower in Gaza City, September 20, 2026
Photo by Mohammed Salha/IMAGO/APAimages via Reuters
This commentary was originally published by The Hill on September 22, 2026.
Israelis are still debating whether the recent report is true—whether the United Arab Emirates warned Israel of an imminent Hamas attack roughly 10 days before the Oct. 7 massacre.
But fixating on the few days before Oct. 7 obscures a deeper flaw: The Israeli mindset, the strategic conception , remains largely unchanged. It is conflict management. Israel is using a weakened and deterred Hamas ruling Gaza as an excuse to deepen the divide between Gaza and a Palestinian Authority–run West Bank. By avoiding allowing any alternative to emerge, it is sidelining the Palestinian question altogether.
If the deadliest disaster of Jews since the Holocaust should have changed one thing, it was this. Yet, strip away the rhetoric of “ total victory ,” and Israel’s Gaza policy today looks quite similar, just with more bloodshed and rubble.
In recent weeks, Israeli leaders have vowed to remain in Gaza for the long term and end Hamas’s rule once and for all. Following a string of successful assassinations of Hamas commanders, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz declared : “Our message is clear: No terrorist is immune, and Hamas will not be in Gaza.”
Israel is using a weakened and deterred Hamas ruling Gaza as an excuse to deepen the divide between Gaza and a Palestinian Authority–run West Bank.
Weakening Hamas is legitimate, and so is Israel’s demand that it relinquish control of Gaza. But Israel’s revealed preference tells a different story.
Even as Israel holds an estimated 60 percent of Gaza , Hamas still controls over 95 percent of the population. Hamas is both a terrorist organization and Gaza’s de facto government; removing the former requires an alternative for the latter. Israel refused to hand that role to the Palestinian Authority but signed on to President Trump’s 20-point plan last year, which offers exactly that: a transition to the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, eventually leading to a reformed Palestinian Authority.
The Israeli government apparently never intended to let that alternative emerge.
Members of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza remain in Cairo, with no timeline for entering Gaza. Roughly 6,000 vetted police recruits, meant to begin training months ago, have not left Gaza because Israel will not commit to letting them return.
Construction of a base for the International Stabilization Force is stalled by bureaucracy. Reconstruction of the Israeli-held “Green Zone” meant to showcase non-Hamas governance hasn’t advanced. And in the West Bank, Israeli policy is weakening the Palestinian Authority toward collapse and carving the territory into cantons to ensure no Palestinian governance, with or without Gaza, is ever viable.
Hamas has expectedly stalled the plan, too. But in August it accepted the Board of Peace’s roadmap, listing 15 principles for phased disarmament in exchange for Israel Defense Forces withdrawal. Israel has valid concerns, including the roadmap’s timeline, scope of disarmament, and Qatar and Turkey’s role in verifying compliance.
A future Israeli government that wants a different outcome will have to act like it.
But justified skepticism does not excuse refusing to engage. Instead of making Hamas back its words, Israel has effectively handed it veto power over the process, drawing international blame for stalling while Hamas gains recognition as a legitimate partner.
Domestic politics explains much of this. Israel faces a charged election on Oct. 27 , and Netanyahu’s coalition cannot show compromise on Gaza. Even pressure from Trump plays in his favor, as he claims to be the only one who can stand up to who he called “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.” Netanyahu’s rivals, meantime, are trying to outflank him from the right, vowing to keep fighting rather than engage the U.S.-led plan.
But whoever wins will still have to pick up the Trump framework. The alternatives—renewed full-scale war or a Gaza permanently split between an Israeli-held east and Hamas-run west—serve neither Israel’s security interests nor produce an acceptable status quo.
Rather than campaigning on the same hawkish instinct, prime minister contenders should say that the current approach only keeps Hamas in power: deterred, but not replaced, with no real alternative given a chance.
A future Israeli government that wants a different outcome will have to act like it. This means setting a political horizon instead of managing the conflict incident by incident, taking initiative on the Trump plan and disarmament roadmap instead of being dragged along by Washington, Cairo, or Doha.
It also requires letting the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza function and supporting Palestinian Authority reform rather than treating its flaws as a pretext for exclusion and redirecting Gaza’s financial lifelines to starve Hamas economically rather than merely bombing it.
Such a shift could unlock the funding, troops, and regional cooperation the plan needs, and begin restoring Israel’s ties with Europe and the Arab world.
A new government will find it hard to change course quickly. The only way to make that happen is U.S. leadership from the top, because whoever wins will want Trump on their side.
The ceasefire, the hostages’ return, and the 20-point framework a year ago were a major achievement. The Trump administration can use this anniversary and Israel’s election to press ahead. Otherwise, Israel risks drifting back into an Oct. 6 reality: a contained, managed Hamas quietly rebuilding behind a calm facade, primed to explode again.
Shira Efron is the Israel policy chair and a senior fellow at RAND.

“You only need to find one person in this entire world who doesn’t find you completely insufferable.”
That’s the wisdom Taylor Swift dispenses near the end of “Cleveland!,” from a newly expanded edition of “ The Life of a Showgirl ,” and if that exclamation point doesn’t tell you she’s found that person then I don’t know what would.
Released Thursday night, almost exactly a year after the original album came out, “ The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore ” tacks four bonus songs onto the blockbuster 2025 LP that set a record for the biggest opening week of all time even as it drew the harshest reviews of her career. It also follows Swift’s high-profile wedding in July — her husband, the NFL star Travis Kelce, grew up in Cleveland Heights — and comes just as Grammy voters are about to decide on nominations for February’s awards ceremony, where “The Life of a Showgirl” is eligible for Swift’s eighth album of the year nod. (In case you haven’t been keeping track, that would tie her with Frank Sinatra for the most in Recording Academy history.)
In a statement ahead of “The Encore’s” release, Swift said she’d taken a trip to Sweden to celebrate “Showgirl’s” success with Max Martin and Shellback, her two principal collaborators on the album. “Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in,” she wrote, “but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs.”
Here are the four “Encore” tracks, ranked from worst to best.
4. ‘Cleveland!’ The exclamation point really is hilarious. (No shots at Cleveland.) I kind of dig the airy jangle-pop production, which reminds me a bit of “Ruin the Friendship,” by far the best song on the original “Showgirl.” But writing about her and Kelce’s romance as a bulwark against all the hate she receives as a rich and powerful pop star feels pretty uninspired, at least as rendered here. “The taste of me is acquired, but it’s his favorite dish”? Alas, no.
3. ‘Patient Zero’ “Encore’s” lead single — with a splashy music video set to premiere during Sunday night’s MTV Video Music Awards — has Swift fielding a phone call from a woman who’s dating one of the singer’s exes and could use a little advice. (“I’ve gotta be honest — I’ve been expecting your call,” Swift tells her.) That’s a rich premise, and I like the way the unexpected fiddle lick scrapes against the glossy synths. Again, though, the lyrics lack the emotional sophistication with which she once would have told a story like this one. And the song’s central image — a guy with a “devil on his shoulder under his halo” — is downright awkward.
2. ‘Pink Clouding’ OK, now we’re getting somewhere. This shimmering electro-pop number takes its title, as I just learned, from a term used among people experiencing addiction to describe the temporary euphoria one might feel in the early stages of recovery. (Recall that Swift wrote “Lavender Haze” a few years ago after hearing the phrase on “Mad Men.”) Here she’s looking back with regret at a relationship that she can see now was clearly a rebound: “You met me at a cursed time / I told you I was fine / And you were so good / That’s why you haunt me like you should.”
1. ‘Babylon’ Look, I’m not crazy about “liberated libertine.” And “Love is ice upon the ladder that you need to climb”? It’s giving Airbnb wall art. But man, oh man, does Swift finally tap into something deep in “Encore’s” closer: a trembling acoustic-guitar ditty about someone who’s realized only too late what they let slip away. Listen for yourself to hear how she sings it — this is a beautifully tender vocal performance — but the verse about the all-but-abandoned young mom sneaking into the bathroom to call her mom is an absolute killer. Taylor Swift: good songwriter!

articles.content_orig:
The chaos of the final day of the WNBA regular season, which decided three of the four first-round playoff matchups, feels like a scaled-down harbinger of what’s next. We’re about to see an unusually wide-open first round; the gap between the no. 1 and no. 8 seeds is a historically tight seven games. For reference, that gap was 11 games last season and 17 the season before. Every lower seed boasts a little bit of a “nobody wants to see them in the first round” factor, besides the injury-plagued Dallas Wings, who carry the inferior but still scary “nothing to lose” label.
The WNBA’s 30th regular season has also been its longest, and the home-away-home format of the first round (which isn't organized by conference) will guarantee arduous travel for six of eight playoff teams. To boot, half the league is still getting over the jet lag and interruption caused by the FIBA tournament earlier this month in Berlin, held smack-dab in the final third of the WNBA season. There has never been a better time for an underdog to steal a game—or even a series.
I hesitate to romanticize the WNBA’s shoestring-budget past, but there’s something quaint about a season marked by exponential increases in player salaries hearkening back to the league’s adaptive, provisional roots. In time, the first round will be longer, and once expansion is complete, conferences will likely be reinstated as a structuring part of postseason play. But for now, in the messy middle of the WNBA’s ascendance , we are being given the gift of a rare first round where just about anything could happen—which has both its charms and frustrations.
With that in mind, let’s rank the first-round series based on the likelihood of an upset, starting with the longest shot, and examine the postseason race as a whole.
Paige Bueckers controls the ball against Gabby Williams
Dallas is the great afterthought of the postseason, and rightfully so. It has been absolutely decimated by injuries. Azzi Fudd, the 2026 no. 1 pick and the Wings’ best point-of-attack defender, is out for the rest of the season. The status of Alanna Smith, whose rim protection has carried a team to the WNBA Finals before, remains up in the air.
But they do have two wild cards:
I don’t see Dallas winning this series, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it kept up against the Valkyries’ style longer than expected.

Breanna Stewart, Olivia Miles, and Han Xu go up for a rebound
When Sabrina Ionescu told reporters recently that New York isn’t your traditional eighth seed, she wasn’t just offering feigned optimism. The Liberty defeated the Lynx in five (controversial) games in the 2024 WNBA Finals, and the 26-18 record they clawed their way to this season—despite injuries to Ionescu, Satou Sabally (who is out for the year), Leonie Fiebich, and more—would have been good enough for the no. 5 seed last year.

As we found out in their last matchup, Fiebich and Breanna Stewart are one of the only duos with the size, speed, and versatility to switch an Olivia Miles–Napheesa Collier pick-and-roll.
With Collier back in the starting lineup, the Lynx are better as a whole than they were before her return—averaging a plus-18.5 net rating—but Collier adds some subtle wrinkles that could prove advantageous for New York. With Natasha Howard setting the bulk of Miles’s screens, the pick-and-roll had turned into a perpetual layup line for Minnesota. With Collier back, the Lynx have become more jumper-happy, partially because the two-time MVP runner-up gets double-teamed constantly. On its own, adding a little bit of variance to fuel a scintillating offense isn’t a bad thing. The five-time All-Star simply isn’t at 100 percent yet—by her own admission—and her gradual return to form has naturally taken a toll on Minnesota’s physicality in the paint, an area where it has to put forth a full-throttle effort to make up for its lack of defensive size.

The Dream are 7.9 points per 100 possessions worse defensively when Reese sits, and there’s a steep drop-off when her backups, even DeWanna Bonner, enter the game.
The Mystics and the Dream have similar styles. At a time when the rest of the WNBA is trending toward guard play and offense, both are in the top three in defensive rating, points in the paint, second-chance points, and free throw attempts. But in a war of attrition, the team with the most bodies—and, therefore, the most contingency plans—wins, and that’s the Mystics. For the Mystics, the youngest team in the WNBA, this is an opportunity to call shots, take names, form an identity, and prove that they are formidable as well as fun.
One more stat: The Mystics may be ranked 12th on offense, but they have the no. 1 free throw rate in the WNBA.

The Aces, on the other hand, have such putrid perimeter defense that Becky Hammon is starting essentially a one-way player in Stephanie Talbot, who has logged eight zero-point games this season. With Smith out, Hammon will likely have to go small around Wilson, exacerbating the Aces’ defensive issues. Per Synergy, nobody has given up more points as a primary defender this season than the Aces’ Jackie Young. Jewell Loyd, at 11th worst, is not far behind. The Fever have their own perimeter deficiencies on the defensive end, and I wouldn’t blame you for picking the team featuring the GOAT and the title pedigree to win here. But if the series turns into a defense-optional, offense-optimal free-for-all, I’m siding with Indiana, which has broken the 100-point mark this season more than any other team in WNBA history.

articles.title_orig: The US wants the world to pick a side on AI. But for many countries, China’s pitch may be more compelling
articles.title_zh: The US wants the world to pick a side on AI. But for many countries, China’s pitch may be more compelling
articles.content_orig:
The rapid advances of Chinese artificial intelligence over the past year seem to have alerted Washington to the real possibility that the world’s second-largest economy could pull ahead of the United States in an increasingly tight technology race.
“We’re leading China in AI…and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins,” US President Donald Trump said earlier this month.
Trump’s comments underscore the stakes of a US-China tech competition that is increasingly being framed in existential terms. The US has an obvious edge, with pioneering AI labs, the most advanced chips and deep-pocketed investors. Leveraging that dominance, Washington is also forcing countries around the world to pick a side.
But China has a vision that, for many, may be more compelling. Even as it trails the US in frontier AI models, it’s rapidly narrowing the technology gap while championing a more open ecosystem centered on accessibility and lower cost.
In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization – a rival grouping to the Pax Silica alliance that Trump formed last year to reduce reliance on China for AI supply chains.
Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US?
While over two dozen countries and the European Union signed up to Trump’s Pax Silica, Xi has recruited 29 countries, including Russia, Indonesia and Pakistan, to his alternative vision of open models, which allow users to freely download, customize and run without paying hefty fees to American firms like Anthropic and OpenAI.
For developers in the Global South, an inexpensive Chinese model from DeepSeek or Moonshot may be more useful than a slightly more capable system requiring an expensive subscription and access to a foreign cloud provider, said Eric Olander, editor in chief of The China-Global South Project, a research agency.
Amid concerns about AI’s potential threat to humanity and growing calls for a global oversight body, the technology became a key focus of the Trump-Xi summit this week.
The right thing to do on AI, Xi said during talks with Trump, is to “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” – a reference to Beijing’s concern about US containment, from existing tech export controls to potential AI restrictions.
“The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” he added.
This followed preliminary talks last weekend, when a new AI safety notification system was proposed , and the two agreeed to establish a formal dialogue on AI. But the summit has yielded little progress on AI beyond broad-stroke consensus on continuing dialogue – underscoring the entrenched mutual mistrust amid contrasting visions on AI.
China’s embrace of open systems has not always been a top-down strategy by Beijing.
Restrictions on access to the most advanced chips because of US export controls, coupled with smaller capital markets, have pushed Chinese developers toward open models as a way to compete with leading US proprietary systems.
That shift has proved effective.
In a year, Chinese models’ global usage skyrocketed from less than 15% to over 54% last week, led by DeepSeek, according to AI leaderboard data by OpenRouter, a marketplace for models.
Even American firms, from Airbnb and DoorDash to Shopify, have embraced Chinese models, tapping into the advantages of open systems, including lower costs and greater flexibility for customization.
Rather than picking a side, companies – American or not – generally prefer to diversify their technology suppliers, Olander said. Chinese AI could spread through existing telecom, cloud and hardware networks, particularly in emerging markets where Chinese companies already have substantial distribution networks.
“It may not be that DeepSeek or Moonshot will make much money, but the companies surrounding them – Huawei, ZTE, the others providing support, providing technology, providing all the services around AI, may do very well,” Olander said.
The meaning of winning the AI race is also poorly defined. Different metrics, from profitability to market share, could yield a different result to the question.
“Is Apple winning the mobile phone race? Fewer people use Apple products, but Apple eats up 90% of the profits,” Olander said, adding that the likely outcome of the AI race may mirror Apple’s case, where the US holds the profits while China accumulates the users.
As AI capabilities continue to advance, the differences between the most advanced models and slightly less capable systems may become less noticeable to most people and businesses, experts said. Some companies may need frontier US models, while others may find Chinese models efficient enough for their needs.
“For most people around the world, the question will ultimately be about what kind of trade-off they want to make,” said Chucheng Feng, founding partner of advisory firm Hutong Research.
“Do I want a model that costs 10 times as much but is six months ahead, or one that costs one-tenth as much but is only six months behind?”
Still, the appeal of Chinese models may hinge on the extent to which they remain accessible without restrictions, experts said.
At China’s signature AI conference in July, Xi called for greater openness and collaboration in AI, while stressing the need for regulation to keep it under human control.
The more capable Chinese models become, the less likely it is Beijing may leave them unrestricted, said Alex Colville, an analyst focusing on tech and security at the government-backed Australian Strategic Policy Institute.
“Beijing wants to export the country’s technology to bolster its international influence, but national security always comes first,” he said, explaining that restrictions could be placed around AI with Anthropic’s Mythos -like cyber capability, for example, that could pose a threat to China if misused.
“But it won’t be anything as black-and-white as total closure or total openness. What I think we will see going forward is a mixture of both open- and closed-source AI from China, as both serve the country’s national interests,” Colville said.
Instead of a blanket ban, Beijing could use licensing rules to restrict where certain models could be used, he added.
Global developers and some governments have rushed to take advantage of Chinese open models to push for sovereign AI development and avoid picking a side. But they now have to worry about how long those models may stay open, as China may be compelled to limit the deployment of its most powerful open models to “avoid cyber anarchy,” said Reva Goujon, a director focusing on China at research and advisory firm Rhodium Group.
“China’s strategy is only more compelling to the world so long as the models remain available and open so that they can be adopted and fine-tuned for domestic and enterprise needs,” she said.
As Chinese firms unveil increasingly capable models that near the performance of Anthropic and OpenAI’s most advanced systems, Washington has dialed up accusations that China is engaging in what it calls the “ industrial-scale theft ” of American trade secrets.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI have released reports claiming that leading Chinese AI labs trained their models on outputs from American systems, a process known as distillation. In a lengthy report earlier this month, Anthropic detailed how DeepSeek and Moonshot forwarded some customer requests to Claude to train and improve their own models, and in some of the processes, exposed sensitive information.
Beijing has repeatedly rejected the distillation accusations. DeepSeek and Moonshot did not respond to CNN’s request for comment.
